findings.description: The option loop uses `shift 2` for --root/--model/--catalog without guarding against a missing value. When one of these flags is the final argument (e.g. `loa-context-class.sh --model $MODEL` with MODEL unset and unquoted), bash's `shift 2` fails with $# == 1 and does not consume anything; because the script runs without `set -e`, the `while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]` loop spins forever on the same `$1`. No shipped call site (hook-guard wiring, loa-status `--show`, the bats tests) passes a dangling flag, so this is not triggered in production today, but it contradicts the header's 'never blocks' contract for any future caller or operator who does.
findings.failure_mode: Infinite loop (100% CPU, never exits) in a script whose contract is to never block; if ever wired that way at SessionStart it would hang session startup.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the value-taking cases fail-safe, e.g. `--root) ROOT="${2:-}"; shift 2 2>/dev/null || break ;;` (same for --model/--catalog), or check `[[ $# -ge 2 ]]` before `shift 2` and otherwise `shift; break`.

findings.cross_file_justification: display_context_line (in diff) and the skills' context-discipline include both read .run/context-class as 'the class this session runs under', but the hook (in diff) writes a single repo-scoped file with last-writer-wins semantics and no session identity.
findings.description: The class is defined as per-session ('the context class this session runs under') but is persisted to a single repo-level file, .run/context-class. Two concurrent Claude Code sessions in the same checkout (common: two terminals, or one with LOA_CONTEXT_CLASS=standard and one without, or different models once the harness exposes `.model`) each fire the once-per-session hook and overwrite each other. `--show` then prints, and the skills then apply, whichever session wrote last. The same staleness arises when the hook does not run for a session (hook-guard skips, hooks disabled, settings not trusted) while a record from an earlier session persists: `--show` trusts the recorded class verbatim with no freshness or session check. The report's atomic mktemp+mv prevents torn writes but not this cross-session clobbering.
findings.failure_mode: A 200K-window session reads `long` (150K full-file threshold) because a sibling 1M session wrote the record after it, or vice versa; /loa reports a class that does not match the running session. Degraded context discipline, not data corruption.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the session id (from the payload `.session_id`) in the second line and have `--show` / readers prefer a per-session path (e.g. .run/context-class.<session_id> with .run/context-class as a fallback), or at minimum document in the include and the /loa line that the record is repo-scoped and may reflect another concurrent session.

findings.description: Payload reading depends on GNU `timeout` (`payload="$(timeout 2 cat 2>/dev/null || true)"`). On macOS without coreutils `timeout` does not exist; the error is swallowed, `payload` is empty, and the `.model` path is silently dead, so the class is always `long` unless LOA_CONTEXT_CLASS is set. The test suite's `stat -f %m` fallback (CC-7) shows macOS is an intended platform, yet no test covers the missing-`timeout` case, and the failure is invisible (exit 0, basis `default`). Impact is nil today if the harness does not yet send `.model`, but it will become a silent misclassification for 200K-model sessions on macOS once it does.
findings.failure_mode: On macOS without GNU coreutils a session on a ≤200K model is classified `long` (20K/50K/30K/150K thresholds) with no error surfaced; the /loa line reports basis `default` giving no hint that model detection was skipped.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard on availability: `if command -v timeout >/dev/null 2>&1; then payload="$(timeout 2 cat 2>/dev/null || true)"; else payload="$(cat 2>/dev/null || true)"; fi` (SessionStart stdin is closed by the harness so plain `cat` is safe there), or use bash's `read -t 2` loop. Add a bats case that runs the hook with `timeout` masked off PATH and asserts the payload model is still honoured.
